article.articleHeadline: Đắk Bla River Flows Upstream: The Ancient Village of Kon K'Tu and the Memory of the Pandemic.
article.articleSummary: Ancient Ba Na village Kon K'Tu sits along the Đăk Bla River in Đăk Rơ Wa commune (Quảng Ngãi), near Kon Tum. Today it has about 150 households and roughly 700 residents, but a century-old smallpox outbreak decimated the community, sending many families to abandon their homes and leaving only a few families behind at one point; the village name is said to mean ‘abandoned village.’ The outbreak’s exact date is uncertain; a 19th-century smallpox account by missionary priest Pierre Dourisboure (Dân Làng Hồ, 1929) describes a Kon Tum outbreak that began with a Vietnamese parishioner and lasted about two years, affecting priests and locals, though it cannot be definitively linked to Kon K'Tu. Kon K'Tu later rebounded, once attracting foreign visitors for Ba Na culture, with homestays and crafts, yet the pandemic memory remains embedded in local storytelling and place names.

article.articleHeadline: Maintaining a clean living environment: The key to preventing infectious diseases.
article.articleSummary: Maintaining a clean, well‑ventilated living space is a simple, global strategy to prevent infectious diseases. The article highlights three main transmission routes: respiratory droplets, contact with contaminated surfaces, and ingestion of contaminated water or food. Damp, poorly lit, and poorly ventilated areas enable pathogen buildup. Cleaning surfaces with soap and water removes most microbes; disinfection is often unnecessary if cleaning is thorough. To break transmission, improve airflow and natural light, and prevent water stagnation and waste accumulation, which also reduces vectors such as mosquitoes and flies. The piece cites dengue fever and malaria, and cholera as examples of vector‑borne and enteric diseases linked to environmental conditions. It also emphasizes safe water and food handling, handwashing for at least 30 seconds, vaccination, and regular physical activity to strengthen immunity, with guidance from US CDC and Vietnam’s health authorities.

article.articleHeadline: Chronic cough, afternoon low-grade fever: Be vigilant for the risk of pulmonary tuberculosis.
article.articleSummary: Pulmonary tuberculosis in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, demands vigilance for a persistent cough over two weeks or suspected TB. Individuals should promptly visit a specialized clinic for sputum testing and chest X-ray rather than self-medicating. Early detection, when lung tissue damage is minimal, yields cure rates exceeding 90% with standard anti-TB therapy, per government portals. Early treatment minimizes progression to cavities or fibrosis, reduces risks of complications such as respiratory failure or acute hemoptysis, and helps prevent transmission to family and community. Adherence to the prescribed regimen is crucial to avoid multidrug-resistant TB. Symptoms to monitor include prolonged coughing, afternoon low-grade fever, night sweats, and unexplained weight loss. During evaluation, wear a mask and limit close contact. The article promotes the Pulmonary TB Clinic led by Dr. Nguyen Van Tan in Ho Chi Minh City (hotline 0913 805 082; address 005 Lot A, Dang Thai Than Street, Cho Lon).

article.articleHeadline: Unseasonal sun and rain, rising flu cases, should you eat a lot of perilla leaf congee to relieve cold symptoms?
article.articleSummary: As of October 17, 2026, unseasonal sun and rain coincide with a rise in influenza A–like illnesses in Vietnam, with several households affected and some children developing respiratory complications. Perilla frutescens (tía tô) leaves are commonly used in Vietnamese traditional medicine for wind-cold colds, but not every patient benefits from congee with perilla. A simple recipe uses about 30 g white rice, 8 g fresh perilla leaves, 3 slices ginger, 3 small onions, salt, and water to make a warm congee; once cooked, add ginger briefly, then turn off heat and fold in onion and perilla. Perilla tea is another option. However, perilla is not a proven detox, weight-loss, or disease-prevention measure; long-term high-dose use lacks safety data and may be risky for those with allergies, pregnancy, lactation, children, liver/kidney disease, or on certain medications. For flu, rest, fluids, fever control, isolation, and seek urgent care for breathing difficulties.

article.articleHeadline: Genomic Copy Number Shifts Revealed in Plasmodium vivax Isolates From
article.articleSummary: Genome-wide CNV analysis of Plasmodium vivax from Northwestern India reveals CNVs linked to severe disease and drug resistance. In Bikaner, three cerebral malaria and three uncomplicated P. vivax isolates were analyzed using a custom 2×400K tiling array, confirming pure P. vivax infections. CNVs span all 14 chromosomes, affecting 2,138 genes, with sizes from ~100 bp to ~1.43 Mb; the largest CNV (~1.45 Mb) on chromosome 12 covers 316 genes. Large amplified blocks also occur on chromosomes 14 and 10. Notably, amplifications occur in three ABC transporter–family genes PVX_097025, PVX_080100, PVX_118100, and pvmdr1, consistent with mefloquine/artesunate resistance signals; chloroquine resistance markers show chr12 amplification and chr1 deletion. Surface antigens show extensive CNVs: all 24 tryptophan-rich antigens (TRAgs) amplified, PVX_088850 linked to PvMSP7; 23 serine-repeat antigens on chromosome 4, with 19 deletions. These patterns suggest genome-wide diversification impacting virulence and drug tolerance, within an endemic Indian setting.

article.articleHeadline: A disease cocktail killed 32 children in an MP district. The story of Patient No. 32
article.articleSummary: 32 children died in Balaghat district, Madhya Pradesh, between June and August after a cocktail of measles, malaria, chikungunya and dengue struck the region, affecting malnourished communities in Birsa and Baihar blocks near the Chhattisgarh border. Victims aged 1–13 presented with high fever, rashes, red spots, stomach pain and ulcers; Kajal Saiyyam, 10, is Patient No. 32 and died from plasmodium falciparum malaria, septic shock, and falling oxygen and sugar levels. Initial deaths occurred in Matla village, Adori panchayat. Investigations by the National Joint Outbreak Response Team found Balaghat lacked a public health laboratory and key posts (district epidemiologist, microbiologist) were vacant, with a data operator running surveillance. The state suspended district vaccination and malaria officers and mobilised health workers to vaccinate about 40,000 children, identify over 8,000 patients, and admit 745 to hospitals, while addressing manpower gaps.

article.articleHeadline: Meta-analysis blueprint sets 34,975-sample surveillance plan for 14 animal
article.articleSummary: An India-led, PRISMA-compliant meta-analysis translates prevalence of 14 diseases into a field plan of 34,975 samples across 2,018 villages. The diseases include ten zoonoses—brucellosis, tuberculosis, Q-fever, scrub typhus, Japanese encephalitis, Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, cysticercosis, cryptosporidiosis, listeriosis, salmonellosis—and four transboundary diseases—swine influenza, PRRS, lumpy skin disease, African swine fever. Using Indian studies up to 2021, a random-effects model showed substantial heterogeneity (I² 91–100%, τ² 0.0168–0.1400). Pooled prevalences ranged 4–30%: cysticercosis 4%; listeriosis 9%; Q-fever 10%; brucellosis 12%; tuberculosis 12%; Crimean-Congo 11%; Japanese encephalitis and salmonellosis 14%; scrub typhus 22%; lumpy skin disease 18%; African swine fever 19% (ASF caveat: no India-specific data before 2021; design prevalence inferred from outside Asia); swine influenza 30%; cryptosporidiosis 27%; PRRS 29%. Two diseases used unconventional sampling: scrub typhus via rodent/vector sites; listeriosis via food-matrix data. The DBT One Health consortium frames this as India’s largest post-COVID One Health baseline effort, employing a two-stage stratified sampling design.

article.articleHeadline: Measles Outbreak: A New Crisis Deepens in Bangladesh, a Major Warning for Countries Worldwide Including India, the Situation Worsened After a Change of Government — CNBC Awaaz
article.articleSummary: Measles outbreak in Bangladesh represents the world’s most severe surge this year. From March through Oct 9, 2026, Bangladesh reported about 202,000 suspected cases, 22,000 laboratory-confirmed, with 1,147 deaths—94% of which were in children under five. Vaccination coverage has fallen below the 95% target: first-dose coverage dropped from 96% in 2024 to 90% in 2025; second-dose from 93% to 86%. An emergency campaign in Apr–May vaccinated roughly 20 million children, briefly curbing cases before transmission rebounded. September averaged 1,198 new daily cases. A August meeting noted that 82% of infected children were unvaccinated before the campaign, rising to 85% after. A September-end drive aims to reach 3.4 million previously missed children. Reaching unregistered children (up to 40%) and filling about one-third of health posts remain major challenges; about one-third of cases occur in children over five years. This serves as a warning for India and others on sustaining high vaccination coverage.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue Fever Can Reach the Brain Directly; What Are the Warning Signs? Read the Doctor's Advice | Dengue Fever: Effects on the Brain.
article.articleSummary: Dengue fever can directly affect the brain and central nervous system. While typical dengue presents with high fever, body pains, weakness, and low platelets, severe cases may involve confusion, drowsiness, agitation, seizures, and altered mental status. A senior consultant Dr. Neetu Jain of PSRI Hospital explains that brain involvement may result from direct viral invasion or from systemic illness, including liver failure, hypoglycemia, electrolyte imbalances (notably sodium), or reduced cerebral blood flow in critical illness. Clinicians monitor consciousness, blood pressure, blood glucose, platelets, and other tests to guide management; timely detection and treatment can prevent complications. Do not overlook severe signs such as severe headache with confusion, abnormal behavior, persistent vomiting, seizures, or dizziness, which warrant immediate hospitalization. The article emphasizes that low platelets alone are not a definitive marker of severe dengue.

article.articleHeadline: Huge Rural Survey in India Maps Tuberculosis Burden and Vulnerable Groups
article.articleSummary: Rural India TB burden mapped across six districts shows a self-reported TB prevalence of about 150 per 100,000 population. India accounts for roughly a quarter of global TB cases. The PLOS One study surveyed 82,636 individuals, using universal household sampling in blocks and villages, to profile both active TB status and six vulnerability factors: HIV infection (0.9%), current smoking (5%), silicosis (1.2%), occupational exposure to silica dust (1.1%), diabetes mellitus (1.4%), and persistent cough >2 weeks (4%). These coexisting risk factors identify population pockets with higher progression risk from latent infection to active disease. HIV and diabetes notably elevate progression risk, while smoking, silica exposure, and silicosis impair airway defenses. The cough trigger aligns with NTEP screening algorithms for sputum testing and molecular diagnostics like GeneXpert; results are meant to inform targeted rural screening and elimination efforts.

article.articleHeadline: Continuing mumps outbreak in Keralam leads to renewed demand for MMR vaccine
article.articleSummary: Mumps outbreak in Keralam ongoing since late 2023 persists into 2026, with 74,907 cases in 2024, 26,462 in 2025, and 6,606 cases so far in 2026. Outbreaks triggered school and hostel closures in Alappuzha, Thrissur, and Kottayam. Renewed demands to add the mumps component to the Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP), which currently provides two doses of measles-rubella (MR) vaccine, not MMR. The Indian Academy of Paediatrics advocates replacing MR with MMR, citing under-documented disease burden and long-term complications. A September 2026 study from the Keralam NIV unit found genotype C circulating in 2024–25, distinct from vaccine-strain genotype N (L-Zagreb); authors urge ongoing molecular surveillance but caution that genetic difference alone doesn’t prove vaccine failure. Complications include pancreatitis, encephalitis, aseptic meningitis; gonadal involvement and sensorineural hearing loss. Centre cites Tamil Nadu RTI on UIP decisions; NTAGI downplays disability burden.

article.articleHeadline: "They threatened our female employee with death": Styrian on an Ebola mission.
article.articleSummary: Bundibugyo ebolavirus is driving the fastest-spreading outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo to date, with over 9,000 cases and more than 4,300 deaths. Declared in mid-May, the cluster likely began months earlier in a conflict-affected region, hindering surveillance and response. Transmission requires close contact with infected individuals or their bodily fluids; aerosol spread is not supported. Case fatality near 50%. There is no vaccine or therapy proven specifically against Bundibugyo, though existing Ebola Zaire vaccines have shown some cross-reactive T-cell responses in studies published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases; broader protection remains unproven, and other vaccines/antibodies are in development. The outbreak’s severity is compounded by fear, misinformation, and violence against help, including threats to a female health worker and the killing of politician Marie-Célestin Karondwa after he advocated preventive measures. Ground teams report underfunded health systems, scarce labs, vehicles, and extensive territory.

article.articleHeadline: Chikungunya infection has persisted for two decades; Aedes mosquito control remains far away.
article.articleSummary: Chikungunya infection persists in Kerala for two decades as Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus breeding remains uncontrolled. First reported in Alappuzha (2006), the outbreak spread to coastal districts Kollam and Thiruvananthapuram, with Cherthala seeing early deaths. In Aug–Sep 2006, about 70,000 sought treatment; more than 90 died, and by October deaths exceeded 100. In 2007, Kottayam, Pathanamthitta, and Idukki were affected, ultimately spreading across Kerala, with over 500,000 people infected. Severe joint and muscle pain caused walking difficulties, and many patients experienced prolonged pain despite treatment; no antiviral drug has been identified, leaving mosquito control as the sole preventive measure. Africa-origin tracing: Tanganyika reported in 1952, virus identified in 1955; the name Chikungunya derives from an African term describing bent posture due to painful joints.

article.articleHeadline: What is the plague: Yersinia pestis causes 600 cases annually.
article.articleSummary: Plague, caused by Yersinia pestis, results in about 600 cases annually worldwide. Three forms affect different body parts: bubonic plague damages lymph nodes with swelling and often presents with blackened lips; septicemic plague in the blood; and pneumonic plague in the lungs, which transmits via airborne droplets. Transmission mainly occurs through flea bites or contact with infected animals; pneumonic plague can spread between people by inhalation. Diagnosis is confirmed by detecting the bacteria in lymph node fluid, blood, or sputum, guiding immediate therapy. With antibiotics (commonly gentamicin and fluoroquinolones) and supportive care, mortality on treatment is around 10%, rising to about 70% without treatment. Prophylaxis is recommended for high-risk individuals; vaccination is reserved for those with heavy exposure. Historically, the Black Death devastated Europe in the 14th century, while DRC, Madagascar, and Peru accounted for most cases, with occasional rural cases in the United States.

article.articleSummary: Mpox (monkeypox) outbreak persists in Kasai Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, with 31 deaths and 1,236 confirmed mpox cases since January 2026. In epidemiological week 41, 61 suspected cases and four deaths were reported, yielding an annual case-fatality rate of 2.5%. Mushenge health zone accounted for all four weekly deaths and recorded 17 new cases (412 cumulative). Luebo territory reported 18 new cases this week (305 cumulative), while Kanzala added 17 new cases (245 cumulative). Dekese, Kakenge, Kitangwa and Mweka totals are lower; Tshikapa and ten other health zones reported no new cases in week 41. Authorities emphasize enhanced epidemiological surveillance and preventive measures to limit mpox transmission.

article.articleHeadline: The Church seeks to respond to the violence and the Ebola outbreak in the Congo.
article.articleSummary: Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), driven by the Bundibugyo strain, is the second largest on record and spreading much faster than prior epidemics. As of October 14, CDC data report 9,277 cases and 4,478 deaths. The outbreak surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation, far quicker than the 2018 Congo outbreak (≈235 days). The eastern DRC is the epicenter, where ongoing conflict and armed groups impede access and fuel population displacement. The Catholic Church is highlighted as a key responder, sheltering the displaced, delivering emergency aid, and raising Ebola awareness amid the dual health and security crisis. Father Olivier Ndondo emphasizes that “peace and health” are intertwined, noting that years of war have eroded hope for affected communities.

article.articleHeadline: Europe records a record number of West Nile virus cases
article.articleSummary: As of 18 October 2026, Europe records a record West Nile virus burden: 1,926 cases in 2026 across 222 zones in 19 countries, led by Italy with 764 cases in 70 locations, Greece 455 in 25 zones, France 159 in 28 regions, and Spain 141 (64 in Seville, 59 in Badajoz). Portugal has not yet reported a case. Authorities emphasize a multisectoral response as the virus cycles between mosquitoes and birds and can affect humans and horses; public-health, veterinary and environmental sectors must coordinate. Travelers are advised to use mosquito repellent. In the broader picture, Ebola outbreaks in Africa (~9,200 cases, ~4,500 deaths in DRC; Kenya reports a case linked to Uganda), Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (4 cases in Spain), dengue and chikungunya in Europe (dengue in France and Italy; 164 chikungunya cases in Europe, 163 France, 1 Italy). EU data show 510 horse and 591 bird West Nile outbreaks across 13 member states; Portugal reports 4 horse outbreaks.

article.articleHeadline: Sandwich ELISA Offers Rapid Antigen Test for Feline Coronavirus Detection
article.articleSummary: Fujian, China, researchers developed and validated a double-antibody sandwich ELISA (DAS-ELISA) that detects the feline coronavirus (FCoV) spike protein directly in feline fecal samples and ascitic fluid, providing a low-cost, high-throughput alternative to RT-qPCR. Using a rabbit polyclonal capture antibody and a mouse monoclonal detection antibody against a truncated Type I FCoV spike protein (FCoV-SP), the assay achieved clinical sensitivity of 81.3% and specificity of 80.0% compared with RT-qPCR benchmarks. FCoV is a non-segmented positive-sense RNA virus of ~29 kb, with two pathogenic forms: feline enteric coronavirus (FECV), which is highly contagious and usually mild, and feline infectious peritonitis virus (FIPV), arising from mutations in FECV that disseminate systemically and cause fatal feline infectious peritonitis. The spike protein, comprising S1 and S2 domains, dictates antigenicity and host entry, and Serotype I is most prevalent worldwide. RT-qPCR remains the reference but has limitations in variant detection and lab requirements.

article.articleHeadline: Gut Bacterium E. coli Emerges as a Central Suspect in IgA Nephropathy
article.articleSummary: IgA nephropathy (IgAN), the globe’s most common primary glomerular disease, shows striking geographic variation with Japan: ~39–45 per million; France: ~25–31; China comprising ~30–40% of primary glomerular diseases in biopsies. A Microbial Biotechnology review ties gut E. coli enrichment to IgAN, suggesting active involvement in aberrant mucosal immunity and Gd-IgA1 production rather than a passive marker. Metagenomics of 40 patients/20 controls identified E. coli as the characteristic species (14.01% vs 5.54% relative abundance; P significant), with enrichment correlating with serum creatinine, proteinuria, and Oxford histology severity, and absent in membranous nephropathy. Potential strain- and mechanism-based drivers include Type 1 fimbriae (FimH) adhesion, type III secretion (EspF/EspG) compromising barrier function, and LPS/flagellin triggering TLR4/5, promoting BAFF/APRIL-driven IgA responses and Cosmc downregulation, fostering Gd-IgA1-containing immune complexes that deposit in mesangial tissue. Enrichment detectable at diagnosis; association, not proven causation, remains. Published 2026-10-17.

article.articleHeadline: From One Health Surveillance to Mpox and Prions: New Research Tracks the
article.articleSummary: One Health surveillance, climate-informed and proactive, is emphasized for early detection of cross-species threats. The Frontiers in Tropical Diseases collection reports: a multiplex PCR assay detecting Anaplasma, Babesia, and Theileria in 60 captive Gazella bennettii and Axis porcinus in Punjab, Pakistan, with 66.66% hemoparasite prevalence and amplicons of 178 bp (Theileria), 479 bp (Babesia), and 318 bp (Anaplasma). A case study of a 72-year-old hunter with cervid exposure in a chronic wasting disease region confirms sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease MM1 by CSF biomarkers (RT-QuIC, tau, 14-3-3) and neuropathology, highlighting zoonotic surveillance questions. Mpox-HIV co-infection in Qinghai Province, China involves a man who has sex with men; clade IIb C.1.1 (B.1.3.1.1) with no travel history suggests local transmission. SARS-CoV-2 reinfection during waves 2–3: 62/458 (13.54%) reinfected, fever most common; vomiting linked to infection status. Arboviruses re-emerge across the Andean-Amazonian corridor, with persistent malaria and rising dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever; Colombia reports 132 yellow fever cases (2024–2025).

article.articleHeadline: Multiplex Nucleic Acid Testing Uncovers Hidden Hepatitis B Infections in
article.articleSummary: China-based cross-sectional study (1,202 participants: 802 people who use drugs in Yunnan, 400 men who have sex with men in Beijing) evaluated HIV, HBV, and HCV with a single multiplex NAT detecting HIV-1/2 RNA, HCV RNA, and HBV DNA, alongside standard serology. Final status combined serology, orthogonal confirmatory tests (HBV DNA and HCV RNA via cobas 5800; HIV RNA via Abbott m2000), epidemiology, and symptoms. HBV occult infection: 58 infections; serology flagged 46; multiplex NAT added 14 reactive; 12 confirmed occult; 2 false positives. All 12 were anti-HBc positive; eight isolated anti-HBc; four with anti-HBs; HBV DNA mostly below LOQ (one 60.2 IU/mL). HCV: 307 anti-HCV reactive; 199 RNA-positive; 108 RNA-negative; 3 anti-HCV reactive samples failed confirmation. HIV: 170 cases; all antibody-positive; 91 RNA-positive (incomplete suppression); 79 RNA-negative (suppressed). Incremental yield for occult HBV ≈1 in 100 tests. Acceptance high among target communities. (as of 2026-10-17)

article.articleHeadline: Women scientists are reshaping the fight against malaria
article.articleSummary: Frontiers in Malaria editors argue that women have shaped malaria research from its late-19th-century beginnings to today. The piece traces a lineage of female contributors—Anna Fraentzel Celli (Italy), Ann Bishop, Ernestine H.B. Thurman (United States), Mabel Mackerras, Ruth Nussenzweig, and Tu Youyou—who advanced public health, vector control, vaccine concepts, and antimalarial therapies. Laveran’s 1880 identification of Plasmodium is positioned as the starting point in a long thread of female scientific leadership, culminating in Tu Youyou’s Nobel Prize for artemisinin. Today, advances in next-generation sequencing, single-cell and stem cell technologies, gene editing, imaging, and MalariaGEN databases reveal vast parasite and vector diversity, informing models of transmission. Yet control has plateaued amid rising drug and insecticide resistance. The mosquito vector remains central, with research integrating regulatory gene expression, oocyst development, and host–vector transmission models, in the context of climate change and globalization across regions including China, Italy, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

article.articleSummary: Citrus yellow vein clearing virus (CYVCV) has been detected recently in Spain and Italy, posing new challenges for Mediterranean citriculture. The program covers emergence and global spread, risks to the Mediterranean citrus sector, advances in diagnostics, genetic diversity, molecular basis, host–virus interactions, and integrated management with new control technologies. Participants include Francesco Di Serio (Institute for Sustainable Plant Protection, Italy) and Chinese researchers Mengji Cao and Xuedong Liu (Citrus Research Institute, Southwest University). article.articleHeadline: Camel Milk Powder Calms Chicken Blood Cells and Fights E. coli in Broilers
article.articleSummary: Camel milk powder as a feed additive reduces E. coli O78–induced avian colibacillosis in Cobb broilers. In a 35-day study from China, Pakistan, and South Korea, 240 chicks were allocated to Control, Infected, or Infected plus 5 g/kg (T1) or 10 g/kg (T2) camel milk powder. Infection caused depression, diarrhea, and mortality <5%; camel milk lessened severity. Growth declined with infection, but T1 outperformed T2 in feed intake, weight gain, and feed conversion. Duodenal villi were longer in T2; liver histology was better preserved in supplemented groups. Hb and packed cell volume fell with infection and rose with camel milk; RBC/WBC counts rose in infection but normalized with supplementation. Blood and cecal E. coli rose by day 21–35 in Infected but fell with milk, especially in T2. The study notes camel milk’s bioactive components and immune modulation in erythrocytes as a non-antibiotic strategy amid resistance concerns and EU growth-promoter restrictions.

article.articleHeadline: Machine learning model forecasts respiratory disease activity despite
article.articleSummary: Guangzhou, China-based study analyzed 1004 days of national sentinel-hospital surveillance (Nov 1, 2023–Jul 31, 2026) for influenza, COVID-19 and Mycoplasma pneumoniae, with fever-clinic visits and meteorology. To handle a persistent two-day reporting lag, researchers built a lag-aware XGBoost model forecasting the seven-day-ahead increment using only observable data, anchored by the latest count, and blended with a rolling SARIMA. Evaluation covered 363 target dates within a 371-day window. Results: RMSE 16.50 (total), 12.64 (adults), 6.14 (children); R2 0.640, 0.694, 0.353; directional accuracy 67.2–73.5%; surge-day sensitivity 58.1–78.4%. Diebold-Mariano tests showed improvement over persistence for total and adult series (p=0.001, p=0.003), but not vs a 7-day moving average or SARIMA; in children, no significance. Extended-period absolute-count forecasts worsened (RMSE 20.32; R2 0.453) as fever attendance fell 31.5% and case-to-visit rose 31.6%, highlighting modest practical gains.

article.articleHeadline: AI Reads Liver Scans to Tell Hepatitis B Cirrhosis Apart from
article.articleSummary: China multicenter study enrolled 143 patients with hepatitis B virus (HBV)-related cirrhosis or schistosomiasis-related cirrhosis across three institutions from Aug 2019 to Dec 2021. Researchers applied radiomics to non-contrast CT liver images plus basic clinical data to distinguish etiologies non-invasively. Feature selection used mRMR and LASSO to produce a Rad-score. Three models were built: clinical, radiomics, and integrated. The integrated model achieved AUCs of 0.990 (training), 0.920 (internal validation), and 0.782 (external validation); external drop reflects cross-site variability. Schistosomiasis-related fibrosis concentrates periportal around portal veins, whereas HBV cirrhosis shows diffuse parenchymal damage; Rad-score differed significantly (p<0.001). The integrated model offered the greatest clinical utility per decision curve analysis and showed good calibration, supporting a noninvasive approach to guide treatment decisions—such as antiparasitic therapy for schistosomiasis—in regions where both diseases coexist.

article.articleHeadline: Heat-resistant fungi: could climate pave the way for new infections?
article.articleSummary: Rhodosporidiobolus fluvialis, a heat-tolerant yeast, has caused two human infections detected by hospital surveillance in China. A 2024 Nature Microbiology study showed exposure to mammalian body temperatures can promote mutations linked to increased virulence and antifungal resistance, highlighting a potential, but not proven, link between heat adaptation and difficult-to-treat infections. A 2026 PLOS Pathogens follow-up emphasizes that this yeast remains extremely rare in clinical practice and many features, including nosocomial transmission, are still unknown; climate connection remains hypothetical. Invasive fungal infections threaten immunocompromised patients, including those with hematologic cancers, undergoing chemotherapy or transplantation, or on immunosuppressants. Outbreak risk can be influenced by environments after floods, where damp buildings foster molds; CDC advises immunocompromised individuals to avoid mold and skip cleanup. Diagnosis is lab- and history-dependent; treatment options are limited, with only four new antifungals approved in the past decade per WHO. Italy should strengthen mycology in surveillance and care pathways.

triage.triage_reason: 中国で確認された希少な酵母感染症2例についての学術的考察記事であり、アウトブレイクや公衆衛生上の緊急性を示す情報はなく、気候変動との関連も仮説段階に留まる。

article.articleHeadline: Rufino, the 57-year-old shepherd who works in isolation at an altitude of 4,200 meters above sea level with 380 alpacas: "We are seeing an increase in scabies, lice, and mites."
article.articleSummary: High in the Peruvian Andes, climate change threatens alpacas and the livelihoods of 56 families in Lagunillas, Puno, at about 4,267 meters, where Rufino Quico keeps about 380 animals. Irregular rains and temperature swings strain pastures, while glacier retreat reduces water for grazing; outbreaks of scabies, lice and mites are rising, with cold spells increasing cria mortality. Glacier area dropped from 2,398 km2 (1962) to 1,114 km2 (2016), a 53% loss. Peru hosts about four million alpacas, over 70% of the world population, with fiber exports to China, Italy and the United States worth roughly $121 million in 2021. The National Institute of Agricultural Innovation runs genetic programs using about 3,200 animals to conserve color varieties and adaptation. Practical measures include shelters, clover forage, and a 2020–2023 plan to install 2,300 refuges in highland communities.

article.articleHeadline: Brain Inflammation and Network Changes Linked to Depression After Herpes
article.articleSummary: From June 2023 to June 2025 in Zhejiang Province, China, centers enrolled 74 participants: 50 with PCR-confirmed herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) and 24 controls. Among HSE survivors, 23 had depression and 27 did not, per DSM-5; depressive severity correlated with CSF TNF-alpha (median 14.9 pg/mL in depressed HSE vs 10.5 in non-depressed HSE and 7.8 in controls; Spearman ρ = 0.345 with Hamilton Depression Rating Scale). IL-6 differed across groups and correlated with symptoms; IL-1beta, IL-10, IL-8 did not. Cognition scores did not correlate with cytokines or illness duration. Resting-state fMRI at 3.0 Tesla showed depressed vs non-depressed HSE had lower degree centrality in right amygdala, right insula, left fusiform gyrus, and left postcentral gyrus; secondary analyses retained significance in the right amygdala and left postcentral gyrus only, with fusiform and insula exploratory. Findings link inflammatory signaling to affective symptoms and altered brain networks after HSE.

article.articleHeadline: Russia's frozen hinterlands long been feared to harbour disease risks
article.articleSummary: Russia’s frozen hinterlands harbor disease risks. A 28-year-old Siberian lab technician died this month from pneumonia of unknown origins, prompting containment and a US request for more information; the World Health Organization said there were no signs of plague or another outbreak but provided limited detail on the illness’s origin or potential work exposure. Siberia's vast wilderness hosts natural plague reservoirs in wild rodents, fleas on marmots and squirrels, and ticks bearing encephalitis; plague remains endemic in parts of the region, though human cases are rare (the last in Russia was a 2016 Altai boy after marmot contact). The permafrost also stores ancient microbes; a 2023 study revived 13 ancient Siberian viruses across five groups, oldest Pandoravirus yedoma at 48,500 years, raising concerns that warming permafrost could release dormant pathogens even as human infectivity remains unproven. Cross-border echoes persist in Mongolia and China's Manchuria due to historical plague connections, tied to a plague-prevention institute established in the 1930s.

triage.triage_reason: 本事例はロシア・シベリアでの原因不明肺炎による死亡例であり、WHOはペストや他の集団発生の兆候はないとしている。中国・モンゴルへの言及は歴史的背景の説明に留まり、現在の発生地ではないため対象国に該当しない。

article.articleHeadline: CRISPR Tools Reveal Hidden Genes Behind Tuberculosis Drug Resistance
article.articleSummary: Tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis remains a global threat due to drug resistance; a 17 October 2026 mini-review in Molecular Biology Reports argues CRISPR-Cas is a decisive tool to unravel resistance mechanisms. Led by Yanhui Yuan at Hunan Normal University in Changsha, China, the study surveys CRISPR and CRISPRi approaches—using Cas9, Cas12a, and nuclease-dead variants to perturb or repress gene expression and enable genome-wide screens in M. tuberculosis. Because Cas9 cleavage is often lethal in mycobacteria, CRISPRi and nonhomologous end-joining–mediated editing drive progress, building on 2015–2017 work and a 2020 mBio report. The review notes a 2024 finding of absence of CRISPR genes Rv2816c-19c in drug-resistant strains. Overall, CRISPR-Cas is framed as an integrated platform to decode and counter TB drug resistance amid persistent global concerns highlighted by the WHO 2024 TB report.

article.articleHeadline: Trivalent Antiviral Conjugates Trap Influenza Viruses by Cross-Linking Them
article.articleSummary: Influenza antiviral strategy expanded with multivalent antiviral conjugates (AVCs) tethered to an Fc fragment, developed by researchers from the Academy of Military Medical Sciences in Beijing with Tsinghua University, Xiamen University and the University of Hong Kong. Using click chemistry, the team built mono-, di-, and tri-valent zanamivir-Fc (AVC-Z1–Z3) and a tri-valent peramivir-Fc (AVC-P3). Tri-valent AVC-Z3 showed superior antiviral activity and, crucially, induced inter-virion aggregation by cross-linking neuraminidase-bearing virions, producing a dual-stage inhibition that blocks both entry and release. AVC-P3 displayed stronger in vitro activity and a longer in vivo half-life than AVC-Z3 and CD388 with YTE. In mouse models challenged with H1N1, H3N2, H5N1, and influenza B, AVC-P3 outperformed other AVCs, baloxavir, and CD388, suggesting broad, long-acting prophylactic/therapeutic potential against diverse influenza A and B threats.

article.articleHeadline: China reports new COVID-19 variant SV.2.4; Taiwan CDC warns of risk: detected domestically in August.
article.articleSummary: Taiwan's CDC said China’s southern region reports a new Omicron-derived SARS-CoV-2 variant SV.2.4, a descendant of Omicron NB.1.8.1 within the PQ.16.1.1 lineage. WHO has not listed SV.2.4 as a separate variant, and there is currently no evidence of increased transmissibility, immune escape, or risk of severe disease or death. Taiwan detected its first locally acquired SV.2.4 case in August; by early January, 17 of 51 PQ.16.1.1 domestic detections were SV.2.4 (about 33%). In the past four weeks, roughly 20% of community COVID-19 sequences were SV.2.4, but overall Taiwan’s epidemic has turned downward and is not showing a surge due to this variant. Ongoing monitoring continues. Autumn–winter vaccination started Oct 1; 988,347 people vaccinated, up 39.7% YoY. Vaccines include Moderna XFG and Novavax XFG; Novavax doses open Oct 19, with limited sites—call ahead to book.

article.articleHeadline: Hidden Parasites Revealed in Brazil's Giant and Neotropical Otters
article.articleSummary: Pantanal, Brazil, hosts two otter species—the giant otter (Pteronura brasiliensis) and Neotropical otter (Lontra longicaudis). Between Feb 2020 and Nov 2021, researchers collected 42 fecal samples and four carcasses (three giant otters, one Neotropical otter) from four Pantanal sites: Aquidauana, Corumbá, Miranda (Mato Grosso do Sul), and Poconé (Mato Grosso). Using Willis-Mollay flotation and sedimentation, 31/38 giant-otter feces (81.6%) were positive for at least one parasite, with digeneans in 28/38 and multiple co-infections observed. In Neotropical otters, 2/4 feces were positive (strongylid-type eggs and Cystoisospora sp. oocysts). Necropsies of four carcasses yielded adult helminths. The study provides the first DNA sequences for two digeneans, Alaria clathrata and Cryptocotyle thapari. Spirometra sp. spargana was detected, signaling potential zoonotic risk and spillover from domestic animals, with implications for wildlife health and conservation. Giant otter Endangered; Neotropical otter Near Threatened.

article.articleHeadline: Sonoran ranchers suspend exports to the United States over possible foot-and-mouth disease
article.articleSummary: Sonora ranchers suspend cattle exports to the United States after detecting a lesion in cattle that could be foot-and-mouth disease (FMD). The Unión Ganadera Regional de Sonora (UGRS) says the precaution follows lesions observed during inspections, which may also be vesicular stomatitis. Samples were taken by CPA specialists and sent to SENASICA labs to confirm whether FMD is present, with results pending. About 1,300 head at quarantine stations will be returned to their origin, and exports are paused for 60 days via REMO. If results rule out FMD, exports could resume on October 20, 2026. The UGRS urges veterinarians to strengthen origin inspections and promptly report findings. Mexico eradicated FMD in 1955 after a 1947 outbreak linked to cattle from Brazil.

article.articleHeadline: About 250 heifers will be vaccinated against brucellosis in Boa Vista's indigenous communities.
article.articleSummary: Approximately 250 heifers will be vaccinated against brucellosis in Boa Vista’s 17 indigenous communities during October 2026. The immunization is part of the cattle health calendar, conducted twice yearly (April and October) for females aged 3–8 months, with a single-dose vaccine given by trained professionals. Boa Vista’s municipal teams travel to communities, reducing producers’ reliance on external veterinarians and lowering costs. Brucellosis vaccination is mandatory for this age group, due to risks of abortions, reproductive issues, and livestock losses, and because brucellosis is a zoonosis. Municipal Secretary Cezar Riva notes that bringing veterinarians to communities maintains herd health and ensures proper handling. At Vanda Elias’s farm, 12 heifers were vaccinated this cycle. In Roraima, the state is officially foot-and-mouth disease–free without vaccination, but brucellosis vaccination remains mandatory for the eligible calves.

article.articleHeadline: Respiratory viruses are still on the rise in the country, Fiocruz warns.
article.articleSummary: Rhinovirus, human metapneumovirus, and SARS-CoV-2 are driving a national rise in Severe Acute Respiratory Infection (SARI) in Brazil, while weekly COVID-19–related SARI remains low. Fiocruz’s InfoGripe urges vaccination for priority groups, with COVID-19 vaccines up to date and pregnant women advised to receive an RSV vaccine. Nationally, there is a mild uptick in SARI among children and adolescents aged 2–14, with stabilization in other ages; RSV and influenza B–related SARI decline, and influenza A hospitalizations stay low. Regionally, Alagoas, Roraima, and Sergipe are at alert/risk/high risk in the last two weeks, with growth over six weeks, mainly among youths; in Alagoas and Sergipe the rise is linked to hMPV, while Roraima lacks enough data to identify the virus. Five states and five capitals meet alert/risk/high risk without sustained long-term growth. Mortality remains higher at ages under 2 and over 65.

article.articleHeadline: After the rains in Foz do Iguaçu, the risk of diseases: health authorities advise on hazards - H2FOZ
article.articleSummary: After heavy rains in Foz do Iguaçu, floods raise the risk of water- and foodborne diseases. Transmission occurs via contaminated water or food, or contact with infected people, animals, or objects; acute diarrhea risks dehydration in children. Diseases mentioned include diarrhea, leptospirosis, and hepatitis A. The CIEVS-Fronteira issued guidance to reduce contamination: store foods in clean, elevated areas; check origin, shelf-life, and hygiene; refrigerate perishables below 5°C or heat above 60°C; separate raw from cooked items; discard anything that touched floodwater. Inspect household water and sanitize the cistern with gloves and rubber boots, avoiding soap and using disinfectant per health guidelines; repeat cleaning every six months or when risk exists. If drinking water is interrupted, filter, boil, or chemically disinfect; sodium hypochlorite 2.5%: 1 L = 2 drops; 2 L = 4; 10 L = 20 drops; wait 30 minutes; use within 24 hours. Heightened precautions during rains and floods are advised.

article.articleHeadline: Tamil Nadu to study dengue vaccine's effectiveness in Kadayanallur
article.articleSummary: Tamil Nadu will study the dengue vaccine Qdenga in Kadayanallur to gauge its effectiveness against the prevailing dengue virus. Health Minister K. G. Arunraj announced a field study to assess the vaccine’s performance and to examine protection from mosquito bites using various repellents and electric vapourisers. The two-dose schedule, with a three-month gap, is cited as providing about 80–90% protection. The Japan-based developer received WHO prequalification, and the vaccine was approved by India’s CDSCO in July, marking its first introduction in Tamil Nadu and Kadayanallur chosen due to a history of dengue cases and deaths. The vaccine has been approved in over 40 countries, including Indonesia and Thailand, with Brazil incorporating it into its immunisation schedule. The program also included appointing 30 nurses; other officials attended.

article.articleHeadline: Wolbachia method against arboviral diseases begins to be implemented in Ceará.
article.articleSummary: As of 13 October 2026, the Brazilian municipalities of Eusébio and Maranguape in Ceará began implementing the Wolbachia Method to curb dengue, Zika, and chikungunya. The program, led by Fiocruz in partnership with the Ministry of Health and operated by Wolbito do Brasil, uses Aedes aegypti mosquitoes carrying the Wolbachia bacteria, which inhibits arbovirus development and reduces transmission. In Eusébio, the Wolbachia Nucleus opened in Lagoinha, aiming to reach about 32,000 residents across nine neighborhoods. In Maranguape, the launch occurred at the IFCE campus, with a plan to deploy 1,900 Egg Release Devices per week, reaching over 67,000 people. After initial communications campaigns, controlled releases will be followed by technical and epidemiological monitoring to assess Wolbachia establishment and disease impact. The method has shown up to 89% dengue reduction in Niterói (RJ) and is WHO-recommended and ANVISA-approved; 16 Brazilian cities and over 8 million people protected.

article.articleHeadline: João Pessoa Environmental Surveillance Reinforces Warning About the Presence and Risks Posed by Pigeons in the Summer
article.articleSummary: As of 17 October 2026, João Pessoa's Municipal Health Secretariat Environmental Surveillance Division warns of rising pigeon concentrations in the coastal promenade (Orla) of João Pessoa and Cabedelo, near markets and downtown, driven by warmer weather and summer tourism with increased waste. The main hazard is infections from inhaling dust of dried droppings, or contact with contaminated water or food. Diseases of concern include cryptococcosis (fungal infection potentially causing meningitis), histoplasmosis, and toxoplasmosis. Dust exposure can trigger allergies and conjunctivitis. Preventive measures: never sweep dry droppings; dampen areas with water or diluted disinfectant before cleaning; wear gloves and a respirator. If symptoms arise, seek care at a Family Health Unit (USF). Capturing pigeons is illegal under Lei 9.605/1998. To reduce nests, GVAM promotes the four As: remove food, water, shelter, and access.

Demographics: 51% male, 49% female; 88.3% pardos; highest incidence in ages 20–29 for both sexes (women 23.1/100k; men 19.6/100k). A rebound in late summer contrasts with earlier months that were lower than 2025. The data reflect onset year, with ongoing monitoring from the arbovirus panel.

article.articleHeadline: Paraná couple shares what it's like to live with poliomyelitis.
article.articleSummary: Poliomyelitis, once called infantile paralysis, was eliminated in Brazil over 30 years ago, but the risk of polio circulation remains. In Paraná, Brazil, a couple—Célia Henrique (54) and Luiz Fernando Zeni (69)—have lived with polio since infancy, resulting in lower-limb paralysis (PFA) and diminished upper-body strength. The article notes more than 3,000 Brazilians still live with polio sequelae. Their histories trace the pre-vaccine era of the late 1950s, when polio claimed a cousin; Luiz Fernando contracted the disease at five months, and Célia, also five months old, displayed early severe symptoms. They sought care in São Paulo and later settled in Curitiba. Luiz Fernando underwent over 20 surgeries; Célia more than 10 to address leg and foot deformities. Rehabilitation at Associação Paranaense de Reabilitação (APR), founded in 1966, shaped their adulthood, though transitioning to mainstream schooling and social life posed ongoing challenges.

article.articleHeadline: Lapu-Lapu City receives ₱10 million US grant to boost TB response

The ₱10 million is the first tranche of a US$316,000 grant under the Tuberculosis Implementation Framework Agreement (TIFA) and Health Commitment Grants, with remaining funding released in phases upon achieving agreed targets and program milestones. The funding aims to improve TB detection and diagnosis, bolster contact tracing, expand treatment services, and ensure access to essential medicines, with a focus on residents in mainland and island barangays. Mayor Cindi King-Chan welcomed the support; DOH Central Visayas officials and local health workers participated, highlighting ongoing Philippines–U.S. cooperation in strengthening public health programs and expanding healthcare access.

article.articleHeadline: Red tide warning up over Samar's Irong-Irong Bay
article.articleSummary: Red tide warning issued for Irong-Irong Bay, Catbalogan City, Samar after shellfish samples tested positive for saxitoxin, prompting BFAR-8 (Eastern Visayas) to ban gathering, sale and consumption of all shellfish and Acetes species (alamang/hipon) from Irong-Irong Bay. Saxitoxin, a potent paralytic toxin, can accumulate in shellfish without visible signs and may cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness and potentially respiratory failure; cooking does not reliably destroy it. The ban remains in Matarinao Bay, Eastern Samar (General MacArthur, Quinapondan, Hernani, Salcedo) with Shellfish Bulletin No. 23, Series 2026 confirming toxins there. BFAR-8 lifted the red tide warning in Carigara Bay, Leyte, allowing harvest and consumption of shellfish and Acetes; fish, squid, shrimp and crab are safe if fresh and properly prepared (guts removed, washed). PhilHealth also provides outpatient emergency coverage and fixed inpatient rates for seasonal infections and heat-related illnesses, including typhoid fever (P19,500), heat fatigue (P18,135), sore eyes (P16,575), heat stroke/cramps (P12,675), acute gastroenteritis (P11,700) and chickenpox/dehydration (P7,800). Registration is via the PhilHealth Member Portal or eGovPH app, or onsite at regional or Local Health Insurance Offices. The move aligns with the Unified National Agenda for Health and President Marcos Jr.'s climate action push.

article.articleHeadline: Zoonotic Giardia Strains Found in Bangkok Temple Cats, Study Shows
article.articleSummary: Bangkok temple stray cats harbor Giardia duodenalis, strains shared with humans, in a 2015 study across 43 temples in 24 districts. Of 500 cats sampled June–December 2015, Giardia was detected in 54 (10.8%; 95% CI 8.4–13.8). Positive sites spanned 12 districts and 19 temples. District prevalence ranged from 30.0% (Bang Sue) and 27.6% (Khlong Sam Wa) to <5% (Don Mueang, Phasi Charoen) with zero positives in 12 districts. Genotyping succeeded for eight isolates: assemblage BIV (4), assemblage F (3), and assemblage AI (1); all are linked to humans or have zoonotic potential, with A and B zoonotic; AI and BIV commonly reported in humans in Thailand. Feline assemblage F occasionally found in Thai humans. Adjusted odds of Giardia positivity were higher in cats with no human contact (aOR 8.80; 95% CI 2.15–35.98), though this is exploratory (n=15 feral). Methods used SSU rRNA nested PCR and genotyping at gdh and tpi.

article.articleHeadline: Inès, 24-year-old, dies after a trip to Asia: what is Japanese encephalitis, the virus that claimed her life?
article.articleSummary: A 24-year-old woman, Inès, died after contracting Japanese encephalitis in Thailand, a mosquito-borne infection. She was repatriated to Nice in a brain-death state and later died from the virus. Japanese encephalitis remains relatively unknown to many European travelers. A vaccine exists, but its use depends on destination, trip duration, and activities, and France does not require pre-travel vaccination. French health authorities have engaged with the case, with clinicians and pharmacists seeking to understand the infection. According to the WHO, Japanese encephalitis can be asymptomatic or progress to severe illness and may be associated with other viruses such as dengue or yellow fever. About 100,000 people are affected worldwide each year. No specific treatment exists; care is supportive. Prevention emphasizes mosquito bite avoidance and vaccination where appropriate.

article.articleHeadline: Indonesia's Tuberculosis Genomes Point to Fresher Drug Targets
article.articleSummary: Indonesia's tuberculosis burden remains high, with 444 Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates from Java and Papua analyzed. MDR-TB accounts for 28.2% of isolates; 5.4% are pre-extensively drug-resistant. Predicted resistance is highest for rifampicin (41.2%) and isoniazid (36.7%), while no isolates show mutations to bedaquiline, linezolid, clofazimine, or delamanid. Lineage 2 (East-Asian) makes up 46.2% of samples and carries the bulk of resistance: only 35.6% pan-susceptible vs 59.8% (Lineage 4) and 83.9% (Lineage 1). Lineage 2 accounts for 65.6% of MDR and 70.8% of pre-XDR isolates. The study compared ten classical resistance genes against ten emerging metabolic drug-target genes (purine, folate, biotin, shikimate, etc.). Across 435 isolates, classical loci were less conserved (mean 96.47%) than emerging targets (99.24%), with higher SNP density in classical genes. pncA and katG show strongest drug-pressure signals.

article.articleHeadline: Rotavirus Leads Childhood Diarrhea Hospitalizations in Yogyakarta
article.articleSummary: Rotavirus remains the leading cause of diarrhea-related hospitalizations among children under five in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, based on a two-year, hospital-based surveillance (2017–2018) at two hospitals. Of 325 enrolled diarrhea cases, 171 stool samples (53%) were tested with the TaqMan Array Card, a multipathogen real-time PCR platform. Rotavirus was detected in 39% of samples in 2017 and 37% in 2018, confirming its prominence. Other frequent pathogens included adenovirus 40/41 (28% in 2017; 3% in 2018), EAEC (27% in 2017; 28% in 2018), and norovirus GII (11% in 2017; 10% in 2018). Among rotavirus-positive samples, coinfection occurred in 81% (2017) and 74% (2018), with bacteria most commonly co-detected. A key limitation is that coinfections were recorded as individual pathogens rather than analyzed as a separate category, limiting assessment of their contribution to disease severity. These findings underscore the dynamic, multi-pathogen etiology of pediatric diarrhea in the region.
